proposals.name: Decimal-precision numeric result density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of the abstract's claimed results are expressed as precise numeric figures with two or more decimal places or exact percentages/ratios (e.g., '81.88%', '1.897x10^-3', '15~30x'), as opposed to results described only in qualitative or rounded terms. Score only how much fine-grained numeric precision appears in the text; do not judge whether the reported numbers indicate good or bad performance, or whether the precision is warranted.
proposals.rationale: Rows R08, R10, R21 and R33 (all dense_low_card_high) all pack in precise decimal/percentage figures (MAE 1.897x10^-3; 81.88%-88.81%; 15~30x speedup with <0.01 error; 76%/77% reductions); this precision habit is plausibly rewarded by a criterion-based scorecard as 'rigor' independent of whether the underlying quality is actually higher.

proposals.name: Anonymized code-repository or 'released upon acceptance' promise
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how strongly the abstract text contains an anonymized code/data hosting reference (e.g., an anonymous.4open.science-style URL, or the word 'anonymous'/'anonymized' attached to a repository) or an explicit promise that code/data 'will be released' or 'made available upon acceptance/publication.' Score only the presence and prominence of this specific textual convention; do not judge whether releasing code is good practice or whether the promise is credible.
proposals.upstream_parent: author/venue adherence to double-blind submission conventions (i.e., whether this item is a live anonymized conference submission rather than an already-published, de-anonymized work)
proposals.rationale: R02, R08, R10, R13 and R57 (dense_low_card_high) all carry anonymized-link or 'code will be released upon acceptance' boilerplate, while famous-looking entries like R04, R26 and R52 (dense_high_card_low) carry none of it; the marker plausibly tracks 'is this a genuine blind submission' rather than intrinsic quality, and a scorecard rubric with a reproducibility checkbox could reward it directly.

proposals.name: Bolded backronym-style method-name spelling
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract visually spells out a coined method name by bolding, italicizing, or otherwise typographically marking the letters within a longer phrase that form the acronym (e.g., marking the letters C-O-M-M inside 'CLIP and DINO with Multi-level Merging'). Score only the presence/extent of this typographic acronym-spelling device; do not judge whether the coined name itself is clever or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R15 spells 'COMM' out of bolded letters in 'CLIP and DINO with Multi-level Merging', and R21 spells 'SAFARI' out of marked letters in 'SemAntic FieldsubspAce deteRmInation'; R54's 'PAR-AdvGAN' shows the same branding impulse. This is a pure typesetting habit that a scorecard's 'clarity/presentation' criterion could pick up on without it reflecting research quality.

proposals.name: Inline math/LaTeX notation density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how densely the abstract text uses inline mathematical notation and markup (subscripted variables, named norm/penalty symbols, emphasis-markup commands, Greek letters) relative to plain prose. Score only the density of such notation; do not judge whether the mathematical content is correct or valuable.
proposals.rationale: R36 (norm-bounding paper) and R18 (rate-distortion compression paper), both dense_high_card_low, are saturated with inline math notation (ell_p-norm families, SCAD/MCP penalty names, R-D notation, italic/emphasis markup), contrasting with plainer prose in rows like R07; notation density is a typographic habit, not evidence of the work's merit.

proposals.name: Primary framing as a new benchmark/dataset/resource rather than a new method
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract frames its main contribution as introducing a new dataset, benchmark, environment suite, or evaluation resource for the community to use, as opposed to introducing a new model/algorithm/method. Score only the extent of resource-contribution framing (e.g., mentions of curating data, releasing a benchmark, providing baselines for others to build on); do not judge whether the resource is useful or well-constructed.
proposals.rationale: R03 (CerebroVoice dataset), R06 (new segmentation benchmark), R07 (HIVEX environment suite) and R11 (Face-Human-Bench) are all resource/benchmark-contribution papers and all fall in dense_low_card_high; a scorecard criterion rewarding 'community resource value' could inflate these independent of the modeling contribution's quality.

proposals.name: Confident leaderboard record-claim with unintroduced baseline names
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract asserts a new state-of-the-art or record result on a named public benchmark/leaderboard using confident, unhedged language ('sets a new record', 'achieves state-of-the-art'), while referring to specific prior models or benchmark names as if the reader already knows them, without introducing or explaining them. Score only the presence of this confident, insider framing; do not judge whether the record claim is actually true or important.
proposals.upstream_parent: the item being produced by an already-established/experienced group fluent in a specific competitive benchmark community, or being an already well-known prior work appearing as an anchor item in this pool
proposals.rationale: R26 reports 'top-1 error of 3.6% on CIFAR-10... competitive with the best existing neural architecture search approaches' without reintroducing CIFAR-10/ImageNet, and R35 claims it 'set a new record on IWSLT 2014... a new record of 49.61 BLEU score' treating BLEU/WMT/IWSLT as common knowledge; both are dense_high_card_low, consistent with a dense reader recognizing/favoring familiar high-status work that a criterion checklist would not specially credit.

proposals.name: Non-idiomatic / dis-fluent English phrasing markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract contains phrasing that a fluent academic-English reader would find slightly non-idiomatic or awkward (unusual article/preposition use, atypical connective words, uncommon collocations), independent of technical content. Score only the extent of such phrasing markers; do not judge whether the underlying research idea is good or bad, and do not use grammatical smoothness as a proxy for competence.
proposals.upstream_parent: authoring team's native-language background / English-drafting fluency and access to editing support
proposals.rationale: R07 ('While pressure grows, some of the most critical ecological challenges can find mitigation and prevention solutions through technology'), R38 ('Extensive experiments have employed GenNet to benchmark...') and R47 ('has been a practically important, while rarely explored research problem') all read as slightly non-idiomatic; all three are dense_low_card_high, consistent with a dense text-fluency reader marking prose down for something a discrete criterion checklist would not penalize the same way.

proposals.name: Self-described warning/whistleblower framing about risk or safety
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract explicitly frames its own findings as a warning, caution, or exposure of risk/vulnerability to the community (language like 'acts as a whistleblower,' 'emphasizes the need for caution,' 'highlights vulnerabilities,' or similar alarm-raising framing about safety/security implications). Score only the presence of this self-framing; do not judge whether the underlying safety concern is real or significant.
proposals.upstream_parent: the topic's social/ethical salience and whether an evaluation rubric independently up-weights risk/impact framing apart from technical execution
proposals.rationale: R19 states 'Our research acts as a whistleblower for the community, emphasizing the need for caution when open-sourcing LLMs,' and R23 frames its contribution around system-level safety of STOP-sign-hiding attacks on autonomous driving ('perception is crucial for both security and safety'); both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting alarm-framing could be tracked by a scorecard's impact/relevance criterion without it being genuine research quality.

proposals.name: Density of generic templated abstract-writing transition phrases
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract relies on generic, interchangeable template transitions that could be dropped into almost any machine-learning paper (e.g., 'To address this issue, we propose...', 'Extensive experiments demonstrate...', 'Our approach significantly outperforms...', 'Experimental results show that...'), as opposed to sentences with content specific to this particular contribution. Score only the density of such generic template phrasing; do not judge whether the paper's actual contribution is significant.
proposals.upstream_parent: the authoring team's drafting workflow (e.g., a standard lab abstract template, or AI-assisted paraphrasing/editing tools) rather than the substance of the work
proposals.rationale: R09 closes with 'The experimental results highlight the great potential of implicit knowledge learning...' and R25 with 'Experimental results on offline datasets...show that our approach...outperforms previous works,' both stock template closings; R44 similarly stacks generic 'we have successfully increased...Furthermore...can lead to an additional enhancement' filler. These generic transitions are a drafting-workflow fingerprint, not a quality signal.

proposals.name: Pioneering 'first-to-do-X' framing vs. named-single-antecedent refinement framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate where the abstract's framing falls on this spectrum: a LOW score (0) means the text presents itself as one of the first, most obvious responses to a broad opportunity, using words like 'first,' 'novel,' 'we introduce' without naming one single specific prior method it is directly extending; a HIGH score (10) means the text presents itself as a late, already-informed refinement that names one specific prior method/paper and explains precisely what limitation of that specific antecedent it fixes. Score only where the framing falls on this spectrum; do not judge whether the paper is actually early or late in reality, and do not judge which framing produced better research.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (how early or late this piece of work was produced relative to other entries already exploring the same space, and how crowded that space already was)
proposals.rationale: R18 explicitly says it is 'extending the effective hybrid latent refinement (HLR) method' and pinpoints its exact cross-domain failure mode, and R36 explicitly builds on 'a widely used variant... [that] relaxes the norm-bounding constraint through Lagrangian relaxation,' naming the specific class it improves on -- both dense_high_card_low, high-scoring 'informed refinement' cases. By contrast R03 ('the first publicly accessible sEEG recordings') and R06 ('an innovative task...for the first time') use pioneering framing and are dense_low_card_high, illustrating how this framing tracks the disagreement direction without being a quality signal itself.

proposals.name: Raw LaTeX markup and hard-wrap artifacts left in text
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of un-rendered source-file residue visible in the abstract text: LaTeX commands and escapes (\url, \emph, \textsf, \textit, \footnote, escaped \% and \_), inline math delimiters used for ordinary symbols ($>$, $\leq$, $32\times$), markdown emphasis markers (**bold**), literal placeholder tokens, mid-word hyphenation from a PDF line break, one-sentence-per-line layout, and stray leading indentation. 0 = clean running prose with no such residue; 10 = residue is pervasive and appears in most sentences. Count only the presence and frequency of these artifacts. You must NOT judge whether the artifacts are good, bad, sloppy, or professional, and you must NOT let the content of the surrounding sentences influence the number.
proposals.rationale: Pure conversion residue that tracks which toolchain produced the text, not what the work is worth. R33 carries '$<$placeholder$>$', 'BR $>$ 1' and '$\leq$'; R55 splices \textsf{} into every letter of its acronym; R38 shows PDF hyphenation ('chal-/lenging') and hard wraps; R47 uses markdown **bold**; R02 emits \url{}; R10 mixes \%, \footnote and $5\times$. Both halves of the slice contain heavily marked-up and cleanly rendered rows, so the feature is orthogonal to the content it decorates yet is trivially learnable by any text model.

proposals.name: System-branding: coined acronym density and typographic stylization
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the abstract brands its contribution with coined names: count how many capitalized system/method/dataset names are minted (e.g. one-off names, backronyms whose letters are pulled out of a phrase, hyphenated compound names, names typographically stylized with bold or letter-level markup), how early the first coined name appears, and how many times coined names are repeated. 0 = no coined name at all, the method is described only in ordinary technical words; 10 = three or more coined names, introduced in the first two sentences and repeated throughout, at least one of them a stylized backronym. Score naming behaviour only. You must NOT judge whether the names are apt, memorable, clever, or gimmicky, and you must NOT consider whether the underlying method sounds substantial.
proposals.rationale: Branding is a writing habit, not evidence about the method. R55 mints SAFARI as a letter-by-letter backronym plus 'Semantic Field Subspace' and 'Semantic Shifts'; R17 mints both CerebroVoice and MoBSE; R39 mints SSPINNpose; R19 mints PAR-AdvGAN on top of an existing AdvGAN; R26 mints IKL plus two sub-acronyms IUR and ICL. Unbranded rows such as R42 and R57 describe equally specific contributions in plain words, so name-minting separates rows without separating the work.

proposals.name: Length, clause complexity and paragraph bulk
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of sheer textual bulk and syntactic heaviness: approximate word count, number of paragraphs or visual blocks, average sentence length, depth of subordinate clauses, and density of parenthetical asides and em-dash insertions. 0 = a short, plainly-built abstract of roughly 100-140 words in one block with mostly simple sentences; 10 = a very long abstract (400+ words) or multiple blocks, built from long multi-clause sentences with stacked qualifiers. Measure size and structural heaviness only. You must NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the abstract is verbose or well-edited, and you must NOT reward thoroughness.
proposals.rationale: Length proxies are the classic spurious channel: a scorecard with many criteria mechanically finds more to reward in a longer text, while a dense reader may not. R22 and R17 run several hundred words across multiple blocks with heavily subordinated sentences; R47 and R58 are similarly bulky. R51, R41, R36 and R27 make comparably specific claims in a fraction of the space. Bulk here tracks the author's abstract-writing convention and the subfield's tolerance for detail, not the contribution.

proposals.name: Era vocabulary: which cycle in the run of submission rounds
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how LATE in the field's timeline the abstract's vocabulary and reference points place it, judged only from the words on the page. Low scores for earlier-era markers: CIFAR-10/MNIST/Reuters/ImageNet top-1 error, BLEU and WMT/IWSLT year tags, BERT/RoBERTa/GPT-3 as the newest model named, convolutional or spectral or bandit framing with no generative-model vocabulary. High scores for later-era markers: multimodal LLM / MLLM, LoRA and parameter-efficient adaptation, jailbreak, value alignment, agents and tool use, flow matching, diffusion, chain-of-thought, anonymized-repo culture. 0 = the text reads as belonging to the earliest rounds represented here; 10 = it reads as belonging to the most recent. Score the temporal fingerprint only. You must NOT treat recency or datedness as better or worse, and you must NOT judge whether the topic is important.
proposals.upstream_parent: position of the container itself in the run of submission cycles (submission year)
proposals.rationale: MODE 3, container-level position. The slice is strongly time-stratified: R01 (evolutionary NAS, CIFAR-10 top-1 error, 36-hour searches), R08 (value iteration networks, Curiosity rover), R23 (dual learning with IWSLT 2014 / WMT 2018 BLEU records), R24 and R60 (BERT/RoBERTa knowledge injection), R18 (spectral clustering on MNIST and Reuters) all read as early rounds, while R29, R14, R51, R12 and R48 carry the late-round MLLM/LoRA/jailbreak/agent vocabulary. Era is a property of when the container ran, not of the work, but it leaves an unmistakable lexical trace that any text model can key on. Tagged mixed because norms for evidence genuinely tightened across cycles, so the parent plausibly touches real quality too.

proposals.name: Late-arrival riff: patching named incumbents in a crowded line
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the abstract positions itself as an increment on an already-crowded line of prior attempts, rather than as an opening move on a fresh problem. High-scoring fingerprints: naming a specific prior method and extending or repairing it; phrases of the form 'previous methods attempted X, however'; describing the existing literature as a set of variants; conceding that the obvious approaches are taken and claiming the remaining gap; the contribution being an added mechanism, stage, or regularizer bolted onto a named predecessor. Low-scoring fingerprints: the problem is introduced as barely explored or newly posed, with few or no named incumbents to displace. 0 = reads as one of the first, most obvious readings of its problem; 10 = reads as a late entry written by someone who has already seen the obvious takes taken. Score the positioning only. You must NOT judge whether incremental or foundational work is more valuable.
proposals.upstream_parent: position of the item in the entry stream / how crowded the topic wave already was when it was written
proposals.rationale: MODE 3, item-level position. R44 states outright that 'previous methods attempted to address this limitation by adding pitch features... However, pitch alone cannot', which is a textbook late-arrival riff; R20 explicitly contrasts itself with 'the emergence of various decoder refinement variants'; R47 opens on 'existing approaches often rely on CLIP or its variants'; R19 extends the named AdvGAN with one extra iteration mechanism; R51 composes already-trained LoRA modules. Against these, R57 and R42 pose problems with almost no incumbents to patch. Crowding is a fact about the stream, not about the item's merit, yet it dictates the concessive rhetoric a scorecard reads as either weakness or careful scholarship.

proposals.name: Elevated-thesaurus academic register and non-idiomatic phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of formal, thesaurus-elevated, or non-idiomatic academic register: words such as 'nonetheless', 'endeavor', 'commendable', 'prevailing', 'intricate', 'efficacy', 'whilst', 'thereby', 'aforementioned', 'plethora'; nominalized constructions where a plain verb would do ('the maximization of the objective', 'through the integration of'); slightly off collocations or article usage; and ceremonious connectives opening consecutive sentences. 0 = plain, idiomatic, conversational technical English; 10 = sustained elevated or non-idiomatic register across most sentences. Score register only. You must NOT judge whether the writing is good, clear, fluent, or awkward, and you must NOT infer anything about the authors.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's language background and practice in the abstract format
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. The unobservable factor is who drafted the text and how practised they are in this format; the visible fingerprint is register. R10 stacks 'Nonetheless', 'In an endeavor to enhance the efficacy', 'in accordance with the pertinent theories', 'the prevailing proof accuracy'; R31 uses 'commendable results', 'endeavors to', 'grounded in the assertion'; R03 closes with 'tailor-made API' and 'paving the way'; R26 uses 'endeavors to reduce the bias'. R27 and R41 make their claims in plain idiomatic English. A criterion-bank judge counts elevated register as care and a dense reader may count it as distance, so it separates the two models without carrying information about the science. Tagged mixed because drafting practice plausibly also improves the work itself.

proposals.name: Compute-scale and frontier-resource fingerprint
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text displays access to large or proprietary resources: named frontier or industrial models used as the object or engine of the work, pretraining or full-model training rather than fine-tuning, FLOP budgets or wall-clock savings on large runs, evaluation sweeps over thousands of models or tens of thousands of items, large curated data collections, or paid human evaluation panels. 0 = experiments described at a scale any small group could run on public benchmarks; 10 = the work visibly required frontier-scale models, data, or annotation budgets. Score the visible scale markers only. You must NOT judge whether large-scale experiments are more convincing, and you must NOT speculate about who the authors are.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional resources, lab seniority and compute access
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Resources are unobservable but leave a hard textual trace. R40 modifies PaLM's pretraining objective and moves SuperGLUE 55.7 to 59.2; R06 analyses data from n>5000 LLMs over d=28,632 items; R49 pretrains BERT and UL2 and reports 20-33% FLOP reductions; R04 builds on GPT-3 Codex; R35 runs seven generation models past 11 scientist annotators in four languages. R33 (36 tabular datasets, random forests) and R28 sit at the other end. Resource access is upstream of prestige and of what a text-only model reads as ambition; it is not itself quality, and it points in different directions for the two models in this slice, which is exactly why it must be declared rather than banked. Tagged mixed since resources do enable genuinely stronger evidence.

proposals.name: Deadline-crunch tells: promissory artifacts and preliminary results
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of promissory or unfinished-artifact language: code or data promised in the future tense ('will be made publicly available', 'will be open-sourced upon acceptance/publication'), conditional release tied to a later event, unresolved placeholders or bare 'anonymized' where a link belongs, and results hedged as early, preliminary, initial, or a first pass. Contrast with present-tense availability ('code is available at <link>', 'available on Zenodo and GitHub'). 0 = every artifact is described as already existing and reachable, and no result is hedged as preliminary; 10 = all artifacts are future-tense or placeholder and results are explicitly labelled early or preliminary. Score the tense and completeness of these statements only. You must NOT judge whether releasing code is good practice, and you must NOT judge whether preliminary results are acceptable.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing relative to the deadline; state of completion when the text was frozen
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Timing is unobservable; its fingerprint is tense and placeholders. R33 leaves a literal '$<$placeholder$>$' where the repository link belongs; R09 and R26 both defer with 'upon acceptance'; R10 defers 'upon publication'; R04 gives only 'available at anonymized'; R08 offers 'early training results' and R22 'preliminary computational experiments'. Meanwhile R17, R29, R37, R52 and R55 carry live links. The tense of a sentence about a repository is a scheduling artifact, and a criterion bank that has an 'artifact availability' item will score it as substance. Tagged mixed because work frozen at the deadline may genuinely be less complete.

proposals.name: Template scaffolding: enumerated connectives and uniform cadence
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of visible drafting scaffolding: explicit enumeration of contributions ('Firstly... Secondly', 'first... then... finally', '(1)... (2)... (3)'), a dense chain of formal discourse connectives ('Specifically', 'Moreover', 'Furthermore', 'Additionally', 'To address these issues', 'In this work'), a two-component method presented as exactly two symmetrically described parts, tricolon phrasing, near-uniform sentence lengths, and recurring intensifier boilerplate ('comprehensive', 'extensive experiments', 'consistently outperforms', 'significant improvements'). 0 = the abstract moves without enumeration or formulaic connectives; 10 = nearly every sentence is hinged on a connective or list marker and the intensifier boilerplate recurs. Score the scaffolding only. You must NOT judge whether the organization aids comprehension, and you must NOT reward or penalize clarity.
proposals.upstream_parent: drafting assistance and editing pipeline (templates, co-author polishing, or model-assisted rewriting)
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Editing assistance is invisible but the cadence it imposes is not. R10 runs 'Firstly... Secondly... Through the integration... Furthermore'; R14 marches 'we first propose... Then, based on this taxonomy... Finally... Moreover'; R32 uses 'Specifically... To improve... Moreover, we introduce'; R11 leads with 'comprehensive evaluations'; R17 segments itself task-by-task with parallel openers. R42, R56 and R57 develop their argument with none of this scaffolding. A scorecard built from criteria like 'states its contributions clearly' is nearly a keyword detector for these connectives, so the channel predicts scorecard behaviour directly while saying nothing about the underlying work. Tagged mixed because a careful editing pass plausibly improves substance too.

proposals.name: Audience-facing peroration and community-impact rhetoric
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of outward-facing mission or impact rhetoric addressed to a community rather than describing results: closing or framing sentences that promise to empower, inspire, or enable researchers and practitioners; forward-looking flourishes such as 'paving the way', 'opens new avenues', 'shedding light on', 'a foundation for future work', 'we hope to advance'; self-description of the paper's social role (a call to caution, a warning to the community); and appeals to broad societal or scientific stakes not measured in the experiments. 0 = the abstract ends on its results with no address to a community and no forward-looking flourish; 10 = mission framing opens and closes the abstract and recurs in between. Score the presence and prominence of this rhetoric only. You must NOT judge whether the stated impact is plausible or whether the ambition is warranted.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience/following effects: the author's practice of pitching to a community and to visibility
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. The unseen parent is a self-promotion and audience-cultivation practice; the fingerprint is peroration, and it is cheap to write regardless of what was done. R03 closes on 'empower researchers and practitioners' and 'paving the way for future advancements'; R12 declares that 'our research acts as a whistleblower for the community'; R30 ends with 'These results open new avenues'; R48 ends 'shedding light on the potential'; R46 states 'we hope to advance state-of-the-art multi-agent research and inspire researchers'; R34 'aims to create a foundation for future work'. R41, R43 and R27 stop at their results. Tagged not-mixed: the practice of pitching to an audience is orthogonal to whether the experiments support the claims, and rewarding it would install a pure style tax.

proposals.name: Abstract length and elaboration
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 for the amount of text, clause nesting, and explanatory elaboration present; judge extent only, not whether length is good and not research quality.
proposals.rationale: Long, heavily elaborated presentations appear in R05 and R45. Such verbosity can predict text-based treatment while reflecting presentation habit rather than technical quality.

proposals.name: Technical compression density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 for the density of specialized terminology, abbreviations, notation, and compressed technical noun phrases; judge only visible extent, not usefulness or quality.
proposals.rationale: R09 and R30 use tightly packed technical abstractions, while R45 combines specialized optimization terminology with formal notation. Entrant familiarity with this format can leave this fingerprint and may also support genuine quality.

proposals.name: Quantified-result density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 for the number and concentration of exact numerical values, percentages, benchmark metrics, and quantitative comparisons; judge extent only, not whether the results are impressive or valid.
proposals.upstream_parent: venue reporting norms and evaluation resources
proposals.rationale: R02 and R53 foreground numerous exact performance figures, as does R05 across multiple tasks. Reporting conventions and evaluation resources can create this textual signal and may also accompany genuine quality.

proposals.name: Submission-format residue
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 for visible markup, LaTeX commands, URLs, footnotes, placeholders, anonymization remnants, unusual spacing, or other template artifacts; judge only their presence, not whether the formatting is good.
proposals.rationale: R11 contains a LaTeX URL command, R19 includes a footnote instruction, and R51 retains a placeholder. These process artifacts can affect text presentation without being research quality.

proposals.name: Promotional claim language
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 for the frequency and intensity of terms such as novel, first, significant, comprehensive, superior, promising, or state-of-the-art; judge wording extent only, not whether the claims are justified or good.
proposals.rationale: R12 and R36 use repeated efficacy and novelty language, and similar promotional phrasing appears in R46. Rhetorical habits can produce this fingerprint and may also correlate with communication quality.

proposals.name: Scale and resource signaling
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 for textual signals of breadth or resources, including many datasets, models, languages, tasks, participants, modalities, domains, or public infrastructure; judge only the amount of signaling, not its value.
proposals.rationale: R05 describes bilingual recordings, multiple tasks, and public assets; R46 spans models, languages, scientists, and evaluation dimensions. Team resources can leave this footprint and can also enable genuine quality.

proposals.name: Recency anchoring
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 for explicit references to recent, emerging, current, or latest work and newly released model or benchmark names; judge temporal-marking extent only, not topical importance or quality.
proposals.rationale: R03 repeatedly frames its work around recent pretrained-model developments, while R46 names current-generation systems. Timing can determine which terms and comparisons appear, and can also affect substantive work.

proposals.name: High-stakes application framing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 for language invoking safety, security, clinical use, road danger, scientific discovery, societal impact, or real-world deployment; judge only framing extent, not importance or quality.
proposals.rationale: R07 uses planetary navigation framing, R12 emphasizes road safety, and R48 emphasizes clinical and sports applications. Subject-matter salience can be a presentation cue without establishing technical quality.

proposals.name: Coined acronym branding
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 for the presence and prominence of newly coined capitalized names for methods, datasets, frameworks, or components, including acronym expansions; judge naming extent only, not memorability or quality.
proposals.rationale: R05 introduces CerebroVoice and MoBSE, R17 introduces PAR-AdvGAN, and R54 introduces COMM. Branding conventions create a recognizable textual fingerprint independent of the underlying research quality.

proposals.name: Crowded-literature positioning
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 for explicit mapping of many prior approaches, limitations, subproblems, or claimed firsts, suggesting a late-stage synthesis of an already crowded topic; judge only the textual cues, not novelty or quality.
proposals.rationale: R04 and R15 provide layered gap-and-taxonomy positioning, while R46 maps multiple dimensions, models, and evaluation settings. A late-arriving or highly exposed entrant may write this way, and that exposure can also support genuine quality.

proposals.name: Abstract length and detail
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much text volume, paragraphing, and methodological detail are present; judge only extent, and do not judge whether this feature is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R10 and R15 contain substantially more exposition, qualifications, and numerical detail than compact abstracts such as R12 and R19. Text length can affect processing and reception without being substantive quality.

proposals.name: Acronym and branding density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract uses named methods, acronyms, camel-case labels, and branded component names; judge only extent, and do not judge whether this feature is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R03, R16, R38, and R41 use several highly branded method and component names. Authorial naming practice can shape text-model responses and may also reflect genuine organizational skill, so this is a mixed nuisance.

proposals.name: Numeric result density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract contains exact percentages, decimals, benchmark counts, dataset counts, speed figures, or comparative numerical results; judge only extent, and do not judge whether this feature is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R02, R15, and R58 prominently foreground exact gains, accuracies, speeds, and resource figures, while other abstracts use few numbers. Numerical presentation conventions can attract attention independently of substantive quality.

proposals.name: Source-format artifacts
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much visible LaTeX commands, equations, italics, bold markup, footnotes, URLs, or placeholder delimiters appear; judge only extent, and do not judge whether this feature is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R10 contain extensive mathematical and formatting notation, while R38 and R59 include conspicuous markup and footnote artifacts. These source-format traces can influence text processing without representing quality.

proposals.name: Prior-work anchoring
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract names prior systems, canonical benchmarks, historical methods, or explicit baselines and lineage; judge only extent, and do not judge whether this feature is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R02, R44, and R52 anchor their contributions to recognizable models, benchmarks, and established baselines. Community embeddedness may affect textual reception and may also accompany genuinely stronger research practice, making this mixed.

proposals.name: Public-release rhetoric
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract emphasizes code, data, demos, APIs, public availability, practitioner use, or broad societal and application impact; judge only extent, and do not judge whether this feature is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R16, R17, R48, and R54 prominently advertise public resources, demos, APIs, or practical impact. Audience-facing presentation can influence text-model impressions independently of the underlying contribution.

proposals.name: Fashionable topic markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract uses currently prominent field labels such as foundation model, agent, alignment, multimodal, generative AI, or large language model; judge only extent, and do not judge whether this feature is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R14, R26, R35, and R38 repeatedly use prominent contemporary framing around foundation, multimodal, and large-language models. Topic fashion can alter attention without itself being a quality property.

proposals.name: Revision seams and residue
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract contains literal placeholders, unresolved naming, inconsistent terminology, abrupt joins, or other visible editing residue; judge only extent, and do not judge whether this feature is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R17 includes an anonymized code-link construction, R30 retains a placeholder, and R51 contains a code-link name that differs from the method name. Such process residue can affect text handling without expressing substantive quality.

proposals.name: Polished academic fluency
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the prose exhibits highly smoothed transitions, idiomatic academic phrasing, consistent terminology, and syntactic regularity; judge only extent, and do not judge whether this feature is good or bad.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing assistance or authorial writing practice
proposals.rationale: R13 and R54 show strongly standardized academic transitions and terminology, whereas R15 and R23 contain more uneven phrasing. Editing and writing practice can influence text-model behavior and may also genuinely improve communication, so this is mixed.

proposals.name: Prompt-obvious framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract follows an immediately recognizable pattern of stating a familiar limitation, introducing a direct named fix, and closing with conventional experiments; judge only extent, and do not judge whether this feature is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R04 and R24 closely follow a canonical problem-limitation-solution-experiment template, as does R31 in a more specialized setting. This textual fingerprint plausibly resembles an early, prompt-obvious entry position, although actual position is unseen.

proposals.name: Templated Transition and Signposting Phrases
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract relies on standard, formulaic academic transitions and signposting phrases (e.g., 'To address this issue', 'Specifically,', 'Extensive experiments demonstrate', 'State-of-the-art', 'In this paper, we propose'). 0 means no formulaic phrases, 10 means heavy reliance on them. Do not judge whether this is good.
proposals.rationale: Practised authors often write heavily signposted abstracts that perfectly satisfy a scorecard's structural criteria. Abstracts like R04 and R25 use highly conventional formulaic transitions, which might impress a scorecard model without reflecting actual underlying scientific quality, leading to dense_low_card_high disagreements.

proposals.name: Visible LaTeX Formatting Artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the text contains raw LaTeX markup or artifacts that were not compiled to plain text (e.g., \textit{}, \textsf{}, \url{}, $...$, ~, \%). 0 means completely clean plain text, 10 means heavily cluttered with raw markup. Do not judge if this is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Raw LaTeX artifacts (R02, R09, R25) act as a surface-level orthographic quirk. These typographical errors might distract an end-to-end dense model from perceiving the text's actual quality, while a scorecard model evaluates the underlying words regardless of the formatting corruption.

proposals.name: Contemporary Buzzword Concentration
proposals.instruction: Score how saturated the abstract is with highly contemporary, trending acronyms and model names (e.g., LLM, GPT-4o, LoRA, CLIP, Diffusion, PaLM). 0 means no trending buzzwords, 10 means extremely dense with them. Do not judge if the topic is good.
proposals.rationale: Papers riding the wave of trending topics often pack their abstracts with buzzwords (R06, R08, R33). This upstream bandwagon effect leaves a clear textual fingerprint that may inflate scorecard 'relevance' or 'novelty' scores, biasing evaluations independently of the actual methodological quality.

proposals.name: Benchmark/Dataset Introduction Framing
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract positions its main contribution as introducing a new benchmark, dataset, or evaluation suite rather than a new algorithm. 0 means it strictly proposes a method, 10 means it primarily introduces a benchmark/dataset. Do not judge whether benchmarks are valuable.
proposals.rationale: Introducing a benchmark often reads like a late-arriving riff that capitalizes on already popular models. Abstracts like R11, R26, and R50 frame themselves this way, which often impresses scorecard criteria for 'impact' or 'utility' while adding less novel methodological quality.

proposals.name: Explicit Reproducibility and Code Pledges
proposals.instruction: Score how much the abstract explicitly promises that code, data, or models are open-sourced or will be released upon acceptance (e.g., 'Code is available at...', 'Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance'). 0 means no mention, 10 means a strong, explicit pledge. Do not judge if open-sourcing is good.
proposals.rationale: The inclusion of explicit, often boilerplate pledges for code release (R06, R11, R25) is an upstream artifact of modern academic submission norms. This predictable fingerprint easily satisfies scorecard 'reproducibility' criteria without changing the actual scientific quality of the abstract's core text.

proposals.name: Named System or Acronym Prominence
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract introduces and emphasizes a specific, capitalized system name or catchy acronym for its method (e.g., 'LoraHub', 'SAFARI', 'MONeT'). 0 means no named system, 10 means the text revolves around the name. Do not judge if the name is clever.
proposals.rationale: Branding a system with a catchy acronym (R08, R09, R25) is a marketing habit that leaves a heavy typographic fingerprint. Scorecard models might mistake this forced clarity for a well-defined contribution, spuriously inflating scores independently of quality.

proposals.name: Appeals to Mathematical Theory
proposals.instruction: Score how much the text explicitly invokes formal mathematical theory, proofs, or theorems to justify its claims (e.g., 'We provide theoretical guarantees', 'Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem'). 0 means no mention of theory, 10 means heavy reliance. Do not judge if the theory is correct.
proposals.rationale: Theoretical fields often condition authors to explicitly invoke proofs and bounds (R23, R27, R46). The mere mention of theory is a textual fingerprint of subfield norms that easily satisfies a scorecard's 'rigor' criterion, regardless of whether the actual method is high quality.

proposals.name: First-Person Plural Action Count
proposals.instruction: Score how frequently the abstract uses first-person plural actions to describe its process (e.g., 'We propose', 'We introduce', 'We present', 'We curate'). 0 means no such phrases, 10 means an extremely high frequency. Do not judge if this writing style is good.
proposals.rationale: An aggressive reliance on 'We [verb]' constructions (R02, R06, R20) is a stylistic formatting habit. This structural density may cause a scorecard model to rate the 'clarity of contributions' highly, acting as a spurious predictor of agreement that has no bearing on actual quality.

proposals.name: Negative Framing of Prior Work
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract explicitly criticizes or highlights the limitations of prior work using negative framing (e.g., 'lack interpretability', 'restrictive assumption', 'inevitably raise a critical research question'). 0 means no negative framing, 10 means highly critical. Do not judge if the criticism is valid.
proposals.upstream_parent: process dynamics on the receiving side
proposals.rationale: Exaggerating the flaws of prior work to justify a new paper is an upstream rhetorical tactic. Abstracts that frame existing literature very negatively (R02, R23, R32) can artificially inflate a scorecard's 'novelty' or 'motivation' score, constituting a structural bias rather than genuine quality.

proposals.name: Generic Field-Importance Opening Platitudes
proposals.instruction: Score how much the abstract opens with a sweeping, obvious statement about the importance of its subfield that reads like a generic problem statement (e.g., 'X is crucial for...', 'X has attracted much attention'). 0 means it dives straight into specifics, 10 means it opens with a generic platitude. Do not judge whether the platitude is true.
proposals.rationale: Opening with an obvious, template-like platitude (R04, R32) often reads as a first-order, safe response written for a broad audience. This positional fingerprint can trick a scorecard into rewarding the 'motivation' aspect of the abstract, whereas it adds zero scientific quality.
